newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries end sharply higher across curve.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries end sharply higher across curve.

text.p: Prices of U.S. Treasury securities ended markedly higher across the yield curve as positively construed data and a well received five-year note sale buoyed prices and depressed yields, experts said.
The benchmark 30-year T-bond closed 1-16/32 higher at 98-28/32 to yield 6.586 percent versus 6.70 Wednesday. Thursday's finish marked the lowest closing yield in a week.
Early on, the market lapped up data on weekly claims for state unemployment benefits, as well as monthly figures on regional manufacturing activity in Philadelphia.
A sharp slide to $7.99 billion in the U.S. October trade gap was seen as less favorable given the knock-on effects for a stronger pace of fourth-quarter growth.
In September, the trade gap was revised to $11.44 billion from an original $11.34 billion.

"(Thursday's) numbers have generally been favorable for the market after getting clipped on the high-flying housing and industrial production data" earlier in the week, said Cary Leahey, vice president and senior financial markets economist at Lehman Government Securities Inc.

Referring to a 0.9-percent jump in industrial output in November and a housing starts total in excess of 1.51 million annualized units, Leahey said investors wondered whether those stronger-than-expected figures would lead to a string of data that showed the economy was picking up steam.
"Clearly the fourth quarter is firming up, but now we know it's not firming up quite as much as some had feared at around 0829 (EST/1329 GMT) this morning," he added.
Jobless claims totaled 351,000 in the week ended December 14 against a revised total of 350,000 the previous week. Claims in the prior week were originally reported at 317,000.
The Philadelphia Fed's index of business activity printed -2.2 in December compared to 6.4 in November. Prices paid and prices received fell and rose, respectivley, to 13.9 and 6.2.

Players said light early volume played a role in Thursday's action, and lead to choppy dealings in the first hours of trade. But volume picked up noticeably at the close of bidding for the Treasury's monthly sale of five-year notes.
The Department sold $12.5 billion of new five-year securities at 6.165 percent, and chalked up a bid-to-cover ratio of 2.79 to one.
The bid-to-cover ratio represents the number of bids received at a Treasury auction to the number of bids accepted.
"It looks like the bid-to-cover was pretty good, unlike the two-year, which was a little tepid," said Carol Stone, senior economist at Nomura Securities Co International Inc.
"The (pre-bidding) environment for today's auction was a lot better than for the two-year yesterday. Claims and the Philly Fed gave (investors) a little breather," she added.
On Wednesday, Treasury sold $18.25 billion in two-year notes at a yield of 5.874 percent and posted a bid-to-cover ratio of 2.23 to 1.0.

Asked about foreign interest in Thursday's five-year auction and the market in general, one trading manager at a primary dealership said, "Foreign interest was supposed to be part of the mrket in the five-year just like it was supposed to be part of the two-year yesterday. I suspect it was there, but we didn't see the bid."
Overall, volume ended up being quite high at $101 billion in late trade, according to GovPX. Thursday marked the third time this quarter that volume exceeded the $100-billion mark.
Average turnover for an autumn Thursday is around $66.8 billion, said Maureen Mooney, senior fixed-income research specialist at GovPX.

Interest was spread across the yield curve, but traders said some issues stood out. Trades in the three-year note, for example, were almost double their average at $3.3 billion compared to $1.8 billion typically.
GovPX publishes real time Treasury prices and volume from five of the market's six inter-dealer brokers, representing 65 percent of the inter-dealer trades.
Late in the day, The Conference Board, said it saw inflation inching higher in the U.S. due to rising food and energy prices. The bond back-tracked only marginally after the news.
